newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka brings battle against rebels to court.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka brings battle against rebels to court.

text.p: Sri Lanka, riding a wave of military victories, has opened up a new front in the war against the Tamil Tigers by charging their leader in absentia over a widely condemned bombing.

Politicians and analysts said on Wednesday the indictment this week of Tamil Tiger leader Velupillai Prabhakaran in the January bombing of Sri Lanka's central bank appeared a new offensive in a propaganda war.
It was the first time Prabhakaran has been indicted by the Colombo government.

Altogether 712 charges were brought against Prabhakaran under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, including murder and causing damage worth millions of dollars. The central bank bombing killed 78 people and wounded at least 500.

"A publicity campaign could well be the real intention of the government," said Rajavarothiam Sampanthan, who is secretary-general of the Tamil United Liberation Front (TULF), a moderate Tamil political party which backs the predominantly Sinhalese government.
A military spokesman said the warlord of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), who are fighting for a separate state for minority Tamils, was believed to be holed up in a jungle hideout.

No LTTE officials were available for comment. The Tigers have not denied or claimed responsibility for the central bank bombing. The LTTE's Paris-based spokesman, Lawrence Thialker, said in a phone interview in February that the shadowy Ellalan Force had claimed responsibility for the attack.
A Sri Lankan military spokesman said the Ellalan Force is a front organisation for the LTTE.

"Highlighting the fact Prabhakaran has been indicted in respect of an incident which has caused so much loss of civilian lives and the destruction of properties will go well with the international campaign against terrorism," Sampanthan said.

The indictment charging Prabhakaran and nine other LTTE members for complicity in the bomb attack.Sri Lanka's Attorney-General Sarath Nanda Silva filed the charges in the bombing on Monday with the Colombo High Court

A suicide bomber rammed a truck packed with explosives into the central bank on January 31, devastating part of Colombo's business district and causing one of the greatest shocks in the 13-year ethnic war.
Political analysts said the government might have decided to indict the LTTE chief instead of formally banning the group to prod the West to crack down on rebel activity.
"The government had pondered over a formal ban on the Tigers. This could be the first step in that direction or an alternative to such an action," an Asian diplomat said.
"Whatever the case, it has political and symbolic significance," he said, "If Prabhakaran is convicted, Colombo could ask its allies to restrict his supporters' activities."

Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu, director of the private Centre for Policy Alternatives, said: "The government is taking steps in order to remain at the forefront of publicity that the LTTE is a terrorist organisation."

The move came shortly after Sri Lankan troops seized Kilinochchi, the last major town controlled by the Tigers, and several Western nations assured Colombo they would help curb fund-raising by the Tamil Tigers.

Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister G.L. Peiris said after a visit to the United States this month that Washington was expected to include the LTTE on a list of terrorist groups, being drawn up for completion probably by the end of this year.
Canada and Germany also told Sri Lanka they were taking steps to curb terrorist groups' funding in their countries.
Government officials said some ministers and military leaders were pushing for a ban on the LTTE, hoping it would help limit the rebels' international propaganda and funding.
"Banning the LTTE limits your options and narrow your freedom to manoeuvre," Saravanamuttu said.
"Maintaining pressure on them on the diplomatic front, on the battlefield and on the political front is where it acutally counts in substance," he said.
Tamil political parties supporting the government's peace plan has argued that outlawing the LTTE would rule out the option of resuming talks with the rebels.
A government peace package offers to devolve powers to Tamils through a revision in the constitution. Colombo has said the war has killed more than 50,000 people.
